z3-context-rc-no-uaf-on-teardown: clear_worker_local_caches() at worker_thread teardown (exploration/scheduler_pool.rs since the angr-9ke6b.59 split; was scheduler.rs) is eager resource release, NOT a use-after-free guard — the angr-bjk8 / angr-1yge9.9 framing was wrong and was corrected in angr-9ke6b.39. Two independent reasons a cached RustBV cannot dangle: (1) z3-patched Context wraps Rc<ContextInternal> and every cached AST owns its own Rc clone (struct BV { ctx: Context } in native/z3-patched/src/ast/bv.rs), so ContextInternal::drop -> Z3_del_context only fires when the LAST handle drops, making drop order irrelevant; (2) root Cargo.toml sets panic=abort, so no unwind can skip the call. Generalization: any Z3-lifetime hazard argument written against upstream z3-rs borrow semantics must be re-checked against the Rc-based context redesign (commit d604c1f04) before being trusted.
z3-timeout-test-pattern: Z3 timeout tests: the lenient SymContext::is_sat (and its Python passthrough RustSolverContext::satisfiable) still collapses Unknown->false, so don't assert on THAT boolean. Since angr-03vl4.62 there IS a decided-only form to assert on: SymContext::is_sat_checked() -> Option<bool> (Rust) / RustSolverContext::satisfiable_checked() (Python: bool|None) / RustSimState::satisfiable_checked(), which returns None on Unknown and never writes sat_cache. Three rigs: (a) deterministic in-Rust -- assume an EASY set (10<x<20) then pin the solver rlimit to 1, so the very first check aborts Unknown and restoring rlimit=0 afterwards decides it instantly, no hang either way; see test_is_sat_checked_reports_timeout_as_undecided (context_tests/solver_queries.rs) and state/tests/solver_gate.rs. The rig lives on the context as SymContext::pin_rlimit_for_test (cfg(test), in solving_ops.rs) so tests OUTSIDE symbolic/ can use it -- the solver_build module that owns build_solver_params is private to symbolic/ and cannot be widened to pub(crate) without tripping private_interfaces on timed_check's pub(super) CheckSite arg. (b) from Python -- tight timeout (50ms via RustSolverContext.set_timeout) + 128-bit semiprime factoring with 60+-bit factors, and assert only on WALL CLOCK (returns under ~5s), per TestErrorRecovery::test_z3_solver_timeout_does_not_hang. (c) PARTWAY-undecided enumeration (angr-fs8kb.84): rig (a) starves EVERY check, so an Enumeration can only ever give up on its first one -- it yields undecided with an EMPTY values vec and can never reach a branch that needs a non-empty undecided prefix, or one sitting behind an already-decided query (e.g. AddressConcretizer::concretize_internal's enumeration.undecided arm, which is only reached after a decided range_seeded). For those use symbolic::stop_enumeration_after_for_test(n) (solver_build.rs, cfg(test), re-exported from symbolic/mod.rs): a thread-local allowance consulted by timed_check that forces Unknown at CheckSite::EvalUpto ONLY, after n real checks there -- so the min/max bisection and plain satisfiability checks stay honest and a test can have a decided range alongside an undecided enumeration. Returns an EnumerationFault scope guard: --test-threads=1 shares one thread across tests, so a leaked arming would corrupt the next test. Check-count budgeting: enumerate_distinct/eval_upto_ascending spend exactly one EvalUpto check per solution produced, so allowance == the count the first enumeration asks for lands the fault on the second one (allow +-1 for the warm-model-cache seed, which supplies one value with no check). Prefer (a) when the assertion is about the verdict rather than about not hanging.
z3-universality-parity-test-template:
Z3-universality test patterns for VEX ops (consolidated). FOUR variants used in #[cfg(feature='vex-engine-z3')] tests at native/angr/src/vex/ops.rs and the symbolic/value_*_tests.rs family:

(1) **Python-parity template** (z3-universality-parity-test-template, z3-universality-vs-python-parity): when angr/engines/vex/claripy/irop.py defines an explicit reference (_op_Iop_X — e.g. _op_Iop_Reverse32sIn64_x2), reconstruct the same Concat pattern using RustBV extract + concat_le_elements. Push() -> add_constraint(got._eq(&py).not()) -> assert(!is_sat()) -> pop(). Claripy bit-index convention: arg[127:96] = high 32 bits maps to RustBV.extract(127, 96, &ctx) with same indices; concat_le_elements indexes 0 -> LSB so slices pushed LSB->MSB order. Confirmed for VReverse (Iop_Reverse32sIn64_x2) and VQAdd (Iop_QAdd8Sx8). Examples: test_vec_reverse_32in64_x2_symbolic_matches_python_ref.

(2) **Spec-replay template** (angr-tukg.8): for VEX ops with NO claripy reference (no _op_generic_X). Build a 'spec-replay' reference using the SAME RustBV primitives as the helper but inlined in the test. Catches structural encoding errors (wrong cap, swapped then/else, off-by-one extract, sign-bit confusion) as SAT counter-example. WEAKER than full parity — bugs in the spec itself are not caught. Examples: test_vqshl_16x4_symbolic_universal_unsigned, test_vqsal_16x4_symbolic_universal_signed.

(2b) **Opposite-numbering ISA replay** (angr-sqfj8.143): strengthens (2) when the op is specified by a vendor ISA manual whose bit/byte numbering DIFFERS from the implementation's. Write the reference straight from the manual's pseudocode in the manual's own numbering (PPC/IBM: byte 0 = MSB, bit 0 = MSB) while the helper uses little-endian numbering. The two derivations then share no index arithmetic, so it is a genuinely independent check, not an inlined copy — it catches exactly the byte/bit-order confusion that (2) is blind to. Example: vgbbd_be_reference in ops/tests_vec_permute_mul.rs vs VEXOps::vec_bit_mtx_xpose. Companion trick: before agonizing over which index direction a permutation op uses, check whether the permutation is an INVOLUTION — a transpose (and any full reversal) is fixed under simultaneous reversal of both index orders, so the numbering choice provably cannot change the result and the 'silently wrong direction' hazard evaporates.

(2c) **Sibling-op identity** (angr-0jh0j.61): the other way to escape (2)'s inlined-copy weakness, and PREFER IT over (2)/(2b) whenever the new op is algebraically related to ops already covered. Instead of re-deriving the new op's own lane arithmetic in the test, assert an identity that ties it to two or more PRE-EXISTING dispatch arms, so the reference shares no index arithmetic with the code under test. Canonical example: VMulHi (high half of the widening multiply) is proved by VMull_lane == concat(VMulHi_lane, VMul_lane) over fully symbolic operands — VMull and VMul predate it and derive their lanes separately, so a wrong shift amount, flipped sign/zero extension, or reversed lane order in vec_mulhi breaks the identity. See test_vec_mulhi_symbolic_matches_mull_split in ops/tests_vec_permute_mul.rs. Look for hi/lo splits, widen-then-narrow round trips, and add/sub inverses. ALWAYS mutation-check the identity test (temporarily break the op, confirm the test reds) — an identity that happens to hold for the buggy version too is silently vacuous.

(3) **Roundtrip template** (z3-roundtrip-test-pattern-for-rewrites, angr-p8cz commit 2870a3429): for IR rewrite rules in symbolic::value, must pin every symbolic with concrete values via constraint, then call ctx.eval() — purely structural assertions about RustBV tree miss semantic bugs (e.g. wrong byte order). Use a raw_extract_node helper bypassing extract_into to verify the Z3-emission hook independently of the construction-time hook. Right pattern for any rewrite with dual hook points. Examples: test_pre_z3_extract_*, test_extract_over_reverse_* at value_simplify_tests.rs.

When evaluating a new VEX op: (a) check irop.py for _op_Iop_* or _op_generic_* — if present use template (1); (b) else, if the op is algebraically expressible in terms of already-covered ops, use (2c); (c) else use template (2), upgraded to (2b) when a vendor ISA manual specifies it; (d) for rewrites with both construction-time and Z3-emit hooks, use template (3).
